references.label: Neural Discrete Representation Learning (VQ-VAE) · selected passage

definition.title: How VQ-VAE turns an encoder output into a discrete code
definition.summary: The passage describes VQ-VAE's forward pass: an encoder produces a continuous vector z_e(x), a nearest-neighbour look-up swaps it for the closest of K learned embedding vectors, and the decoder sees only that vector. The scenes follow the supplied text and the Figure 1 caption. The figure itself is not in the context, so the 2-D layout, the staircase and the small grid are simplified sketches, not reproductions.

steps.title: The forward pipeline at a glance
steps.caption: Input x goes through the encoder, is snapped to one entry of the embedding space e, and that entry (not the encoder's own output) feeds the decoder.
steps.explanation:
The passage describes a chain of four operations. The input x (an image, a sound clip) enters an encoder network, which outputs a vector written z_e(x); the subscript e stands for 'encoder' and is written here with an underscore. This vector is continuous: its numbers can take any value.

Next comes the step that makes the model special. A nearest-neighbour look-up compares z_e(x) with every vector stored in an embedding space called e and picks the closest one, called e_k. That chosen vector, not z_e(x), is what the decoder receives. The decoder then tries to rebuild the input from it.

The paper notes that the model's parameters are the union of three things: the encoder, the decoder and the embedding space e. So the table of embeddings is learned, not fixed in advance.

The following scenes take the look-up apart: what the embedding space is, how 'nearest' is decided, what exactly is discrete, and why the passage calls the whole thing a non-linearity.

steps.title: The embedding space is a table of K vectors
steps.caption: The embedding space e holds K vectors, e_1 to e_K, each made of D numbers. An index k names one row.
steps.explanation:
The paper defines the latent embedding space e as a K-by-D array. K is the size of the discrete latent space, that is, how many different codes exist. D is the dimensionality of each embedding vector. So there are K embedding vectors, each a list of D real numbers.

Two descriptions of the same row are worth keeping apart, because the rest of the passage relies on both:

- The index k is a whole number from 1 to K. This is the discrete part.
- The vector e_k is the row's content: D continuous numbers that a neural network can compute with.

The picture is a table drawn schematically. The context gives no concrete values for the entries; they are learned during training along with the encoder and decoder.

steps.title: Nearest-neighbour look-up: measure every distance
steps.caption: A simplified 2-D view: z_e(x) lands somewhere in the space, its distance to every embedding is measured, and the closest one wins. Here that is e_2.
steps.explanation:
Because z_e(x) and the embedding vectors all have D numbers, they can be drawn as points in one common space. The real space has D dimensions; the picture flattens it to two so that distance is visible as line length. The positions are invented for the sketch.

Equation 1 in the paper states the rule: choose the index k that minimises the distance between z_e(x) and e_j over all j, written k = argmin_j ||z_e(x) - e_j||_2. In words: compute the Euclidean distance to each of the K embeddings and keep the index of the smallest.

The caption of the paper's Figure 1 describes the same situation: the encoder output is mapped to the nearest point, e_2. The sketch follows that example, so the result of the look-up is k = 2.

The rule is all-or-nothing. It does not matter whether z_e(x) is very close to e_2 or only slightly closer to it than to the others; the outcome is the same index.

steps.title: What is discrete, and what the decoder receives
steps.caption: The look-up yields a one-hot choice among K options. The discrete latent z is the winning index; the decoder input is that row's vector, z_q(x) = e_k.
steps.explanation:
The passage separates two results of the look-up.

First, the discrete latent variable z. The paper defines the posterior q(z = k | x) as one-hot: it is 1 for the index of the nearest embedding and 0 for every other index. Drawn as a row of K cells, exactly one cell holds a 1. In the running example that is cell 2, so z = 2. The paper points out that this choice is deterministic: the same z_e(x) always gives the same index.

Second, the decoder's input. An index alone is just a label, so it is used to fetch a row of the embedding table. Equation 2 names the result z_q(x) = e_k, the quantised latent. This vector goes to the decoder.

Notice what does not travel forward: z_e(x) itself. In the forward pass the decoder never sees the encoder's exact output, only the embedding it was matched to. Any detail in z_e(x) that does not change which embedding is nearest is dropped at this point. That is the sense in which the look-up acts as a bottleneck. (z_e(x) is still used during training, in loss terms the paper introduces afterwards.)

steps.title: Why the passage calls it a non-linearity
steps.caption: A 1-D illustration, not the real D-dimensional operation. A plain autoencoder hands the encoder output straight to the decoder (diagonal); the look-up snaps it to one of a few allowed levels (staircase).
steps.explanation:
The passage ends with a change of viewpoint: the pipeline can be seen as 'a regular autoencoder with a particular non-linearity that maps the latents to 1-of-K embedding vectors'. This scene illustrates that sentence with a one-dimensional analogy.

Imagine the encoder output were a single number instead of a vector, and the embedding space held four numbers, e1 to e4. In a plain autoencoder the decoder would receive exactly what the encoder produced: the diagonal line, where output equals input. With the look-up in place, every input is replaced by whichever level is nearest, giving a staircase. Whole ranges of inputs produce the same output, and at certain thresholds the output jumps.

So the look-up behaves like a layer in the network: a fixed rule applied between encoder and decoder that is not a straight line. It differs from familiar non-linearities in that its set of possible outputs is finite (K of them) and the levels themselves are learned.

In the real model the flat steps become regions of the D-dimensional space, each region containing all points closest to one embedding.

The staircase also hints at a difficulty the paper raises next: on a flat step, small changes to the input do not change the output, and the paper says there is no real gradient defined for equation 2. It works around this by copying gradients from the decoder input back to the encoder output.

steps.title: In practice: many latents, one table
steps.caption: Real inputs are encoded as a whole grid of latents. Each position gets its own index, and all positions are looked up in the same embedding table. The 3-by-3 grid and its index values are made up for the sketch.
steps.explanation:
The passage speaks of 'the' discrete latent z as if there were one per input. The paper says this is for simplicity: for speech, images and video it actually extracts 1-D, 2-D and 3-D latent feature spaces. For example, it reports using a field of 32 by 32 latents for ImageNet.

So the look-up from the earlier scenes is repeated at every position. The encoder emits a grid of vectors; each one is matched to its nearest embedding; the result is a grid of indices. Replacing each index with its embedding vector gives the grid of vectors the decoder receives.

The context does not spell out what 'shared' means in 'shared embedding space'. A reasonable reading is that this single table serves every position; the paper also notes that encoder output and decoder input share the same D-dimensional space. The same index can appear at several positions, as the repeated values in the sketch suggest.

A single index among K choices carries little information. A grid of them can describe an input in far more detail, while still being a finite sequence of symbols.

takeaways: Forward pass: x goes to the encoder, giving z_e(x); the nearest embedding e_k is found; the decoder receives e_k.
The discrete latent z is the index k of the nearest embedding. As a distribution over the K indices it is one-hot and deterministic.
The decoder never sees the encoder's exact output, only one of K learned vectors, so the look-up acts as a bottleneck.
Seen as a layer, the look-up is a step-like non-linearity between encoder and decoder. Its flat steps are why the paper needs a special gradient trick for training.
